title: US Pending Home Sales Fall 7.3% to Record Low as Mortgage Rates Hit 7.40%
excerpt: The NAR index dropped to 66.0 in September, its lowest since the series began in 2001, as a jump in the 30-year mortgage rate from 6.66% in late August pushed buyers out in every region.
body:
• The National Association of Realtors' Pending Home Sales Index fell 7.3% in September to 66.0, the lowest reading since the series began in 2001, and 11.3% below a year earlier.
  • Economists polled by Reuters had expected a fall of just 0.5%, making this one of the largest misses of the year for a leading housing indicator.
  • The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate reached 7.40% last week, the highest in nearly three years, up from 6.66% at the end of August, according to Freddie Mac data cited by Reuters.
  • For US buyers: signings lead closed sales by one to two months, so October's existing-home sales will likely fall further — but asking prices fell for an 11th straight month and price cuts are rising, improving negotiating power for buyers who can still proceed.

Contracts to buy previously owned homes in the United States plunged to a record low in September, as a rapid rise in mortgage rates pushed buyers out of the market. The National Association of Realtors said on Tuesday that its Pending Home Sales Index tumbled 7.3% to 66.0, the lowest level since the series started in 2001. Pending sales were down 11.3% from September a year earlier.

The scale of the drop caught forecasters off guard. Economists polled by Reuters had expected contracts, which typically become closed sales after a month or two, to slip by only 0.5%. Instead, signings fell in every region of the country, with the sharpest monthly decline in the West.

"Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates."

— Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist, National Association of Realtors

Rates Did the Damage

Mortgage rates have accelerated in recent weeks. The 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.40% last week, the highest level in nearly three years, according to data from mortgage finance firm Freddie Mac cited by Reuters. Barron's reported the same rate had been 6.66% at the end of August — a rise of roughly three-quarters of a percentage point in about six weeks, enough to add hundreds of dollars a month to the payment on a typical loan.

Reuters linked the higher borrowing costs to Treasury yields, which have risen as the US-Israeli war with Iran fans inflation concerns. Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist, said job growth and income gains can support home purchases, but housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates. He also suggested rates may be near a peak, noting they have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve's short-term rate increases.

Every Region Fell

According to HousingWire's breakdown of the NAR data, pending sales fell 9.2% month over month in the West, where the index stood at 49.3, followed by the South at 8.2%, the Midwest at 6.5% and the Northeast at 4.2%. On a yearly basis, the West was down 15.0%, the South 12.0%, the Northeast 9.4% and the Midwest 8.7%.

The weakness reached even the strongest markets. Among the 50 largest metros tracked by NAR, the smallest annual declines were in Nashville at 2.0%, Hartford at 2.1% and San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont at 3.5%. More timely HousingWire data put new pending single-family sales for the week ending October 16 at 51,947, down 13.1% from a year ago.

A Fall Market That Favours Patient Buyers

Realtor.com reported that the usual autumn pattern still held in one respect: asking prices fell for an 11th straight month in September, price reductions edged higher and inventory climbed. Its senior economist Hannah Jones said the local data confirms higher rates are hitting buyers throughout the country, even in markets that have shown consistent strength.

Jones expects rates to stay elevated after hot inflation data, with markets pricing in a possible further Federal Reserve increase this year, keeping affordability tough through year-end. Yun pointed to one stabilising factor: the limited number of distressed properties is keeping prices steady, and buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until rates move favourably.

What It Means for Markets and Buyers

For investors, Barron's noted the iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF is down 11.1% this year, on track for its worst year since 2022, and said the 10-year Treasury yield remains the key variable for homebuilder stocks.

For households weighing a purchase — including Indian-American families active in suburbs across Texas, California and New Jersey — the picture is mixed. A buyer who can absorb 7.40% faces less competition, more listings and more price cuts, with the option to refinance if rates fall. A buyer stretched at 6.66% in August is likely priced out today.

What Comes Next

October's existing-home sales report, expected in November, is the next test. Barron's expects it to be lower than September's. Treasury yields and the Federal Reserve's next signal will decide whether September marks the bottom of the slump or the start of a deeper one.
